bibliography.abstract: Vehicle trajectory prediction plays a crucial role in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), enabling proactive traffic control, congestion mitigation, and collision avoidance. Existing trajectory prediction approaches generally fall into two categories: physics-based models and data-driven models. While physics-based models offer interpretability and physical consistency, they often have limited predictive accuracy. In contrast, deep learning models provide strong predictive performance but typically lack explicit physical constraints. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Mixed-Granularity Physics-Informed Deep Learning (MPIDL) framework for multi-step longitudinal trajectory prediction in trajectory-rich monitored corridors. The framework couples a microscopic prediction module with a macroscopic physical module. The microscopic module employs a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to predict vehicle-level accelerations from historical speed, space headway, and relative-speed sequences, and subsequently propagates these accelerations into future trajectories through a differentiable kinematic model. The macroscopic module uses an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to estimate joint velocity–density fields over spatiotemporal grids and regularizes these fields using the continuity and momentum equations of the Aw–Rascle–Zhang traffic-flow model. The macroscopic acceleration is derived from the material derivative of the learned velocity field and is spatially aggregated to match the granularity of the microscopic predictions. A cross-scale physical-consistency loss then aligns the aggregated microscopic acceleration with the aggregated macroscopic acceleration, while the ARZ-based continuity and momentum residuals separately enforce macroscopic traffic-flow consistency. The two modules are jointly trained using normalized uncertainty-based loss weighting and an asynchronous optimization strategy. Experiments on the NGSIM and ZTD datasets show that MPIDL consistently achieves lower Average Displacement Error and Final Displacement Error than representative physics-based, data-driven, physics-informed, and generative baselines. The proposed framework also better preserves macroscopic flow–density relationships and macro–micro acceleration consistency. Ablation, sensitivity, cross-dataset transfer, and robustness analyses further confirm the contributions of the macroscopic physical constraints and the optimization strategy. Although joint training introduces additional computational cost, only the microscopic module is retained during inference, resulting in low prediction latency and supporting real-time short-horizon trajectory prediction.

en.caveats: Although the framework is trained jointly using both micro and macro modules, the macroscopic constraints are discarded during inference, meaning real-time physical consistency relies on the patterns learned during training rather than active runtime enforcement.
en.what: The Mixed-Granularity Physics-Informed Deep Learning (MPIDL) framework predicts multi-step longitudinal vehicle trajectories by coupling a microscopic LSTM module with a macroscopic ANN module. The microscopic module predicts vehicle-level accelerations from historical speed, headway, and relative-speed sequences, while the macroscopic module estimates joint velocity-density fields regularized by the Aw-Rascle-Zhang traffic-flow model. Evaluated on the NGSIM and ZTD datasets, the framework achieves lower Average Displacement Error and Final Displacement Error than standard physics-based and deep learning baselines.
en.why: It bridges the gap between micro-level vehicle dynamics and macro-level traffic flow theory, ensuring that individual trajectory predictions remain physically consistent with overall traffic density and velocity fields without sacrificing real-time inference speed.
